Module 1: Data Literacy and Political Science

1 Introduction

Welcome to Module 1. Many of you may be encountering data, statistics, and political science research methods for the very first time. That is perfectly fine—these modules are meant to guide you step by step, with clear explanations and simple examples.

In this module, we begin with a simple but important question: Why does data matter in political science? Political science is not only about debating ideas, history, and institutions—it is also about evidence. Evidence allows us to move beyond opinion and speculation toward systematic analysis of how politics actually works.

Throughout this course, we will introduce AI tools and other online resources. These can support your learning by helping you practice, explore, and check your understanding. However, your own judgment and critical thinking are what matter most. Data literacy means not only working with data but also questioning the way information is presented—whether in scholarly articles, news reports, or outputs generated by AI tools.

1.1 Why Data Literacy?

There are at least three reasons why data literacy is essential to understand politics:

  1. Understanding the political world: Democracies, authoritarian regimes, international organizations, and social movements all generate large amounts of information. Being able to read and evaluate these numbers—such as election turnout, public opinion polls, or trade statistics—allows you to better understand contemporary debates.

  2. Evaluating claims: Politicians, media outlets, and advocacy groups often make claims backed (or seemingly backed) by “data.” Without data literacy, it is easy to be persuaded by misleading numbers or biased presentations. Armed with data literacy, you can critically evaluate whether those claims are truly supported by evidence.

  3. Producing knowledge: To engage in political science research, scholars build datasets, apply methods, and draw conclusions about how the world works. As a student, developing the skills to engage with these practices allows you to move from consumer to producer of knowledge.

In simple terms, developing data literacy means gaining the ability to step back and ask critical questions about the information you see. It allows you to question bold claims, recognize when numbers might be misleading, and engage in political debates using evidence rather than opinion. With these skills, you will be able to participate more thoughtfully in discussions about politics, policies, and society.

1.1.1 Conceptualization and Measurement

Before diving into specific data examples, recall two foundational concepts in political science research:

  • Conceptualization: Defining what we mean by abstract political ideas. For example, what does “democracy” mean? Is it only about free and fair elections, or does it also require civil liberties and accountability?

  • Measurement: Turning those abstract concepts into observable indicators. For democracy, we might measure it through election monitoring reports, indexes like V-Dem or Freedom House, or survey data on citizens’ rights.

Without careful conceptualization and measurement, our data cannot meaningfully reflect the political world. This is why political scientists spend so much effort debating definitions and indicators.

1.2 Story: NGO and Democracy Promotion

Imagine you are reading the news and come across a story: in 2016, China introduced a new law requiring all foreign NGOs to register with the Ministry of Public Security (BBC report). At first, this seems like just one political event. But in the classroom, we can turn this into a story about data creation. To study NGOs systematically, scholars have to decide: how do we define “NGO activity”? How do we measure whether a government is supportive or restrictive? One influential study (Dupuy, Ron, & Prakash 2015, Social Science Research) built a dataset by collecting reports from many countries on how NGOs were regulated. This meant coding laws, restrictions, and levels of freedom across different political systems.

We can start with a single news story and turn it into data by creating clear rules and categories. Once it is part of a larger dataset, we can compare China not only to itself over time but also to many other countries. This kind of comparison shows patterns — for example, authoritarian governments often restrict NGOs, while democracies are more likely to allow them to operate freely. The story gains power when it is connected to systematic evidence.

To build on this, let’s see how data can be visualized. By linking the NGO story to broader measures—such as participation in international organizations (IGOs) and democracy scores—we can see how national policies toward civil society fit into larger global patterns. For example, the bar plot below shows the average IGO membership count for five selected states: (“United States of America”, “Singapore”, “India”, “China”, “Kenya”)

1.2.1 IGO Participation by Country in 2000

This bar chart shows how many international organizations each country belongs to. Countries with high levels of IGO (intergovernmental organization) participation often face greater international expectations regarding their treatment of NGOs and democratic practices. This connects back to the China example: maintaining extensive international ties while restricting NGOs at home illustrates the tension between domestic control and global integration.

1.2.2 IGO Participation Level and Democracy

This line chart compares trends in democracy (v2x_polyarchy) with levels of IGO participation. If a country’s democracy score rises along with IGO participation, it suggests democratization and international engagement may reinforce one another. If democracy declines while IGO participation stays high, it echoes the NGO story—international connections exist, but domestic freedoms are restricted.

Together, these plots demonstrate how political scientists transform individual stories into measurable patterns. The NGO case becomes part of a wider picture that links democracy, NGOs, and international cooperation.

Reflection on NGO and Democracy Promotion

  • Why might governments view NGOs as both helpful and threatening?
  • How could we measure the presence or influence of NGOs in a dataset?
  • Looking at the plots: what patterns do you notice about IGO participation and democracy over time?
  • Do you think higher democracy scores always lead to higher IGO participation levels?

2 Understanding Political Data

2.1 From Stories to Data Structures

The NGO example and the plots above showed how a single event can be turned into measurable evidence. To deepen this idea, you already learned in class about how datasets are constructed, we now turn to the structure and meaning of political data. This transition matters for developing data literacy: single stories become entry points into larger datasets, and those datasets are not random collections of numbers but carefully designed representations of the political world. To interpret them, we need to ask: Where did the data come from? How was it created? What does it actually measure?

The NGO example and the plots showed how a single event can be turned into measurable evidence. To deepen this idea, we now turn to the structure and meaning of political data. This shift is important for data literacy: single stories become entry points into larger datasets, and those datasets are not just random numbers but carefully designed representations of the political world. To interpret them, we need to ask: Where did the data come from? How was it created? What does it actually measure?

2.1.1 Democracy Indexes

There are many different approaches to conceptualizing and measuring democracy, and understanding these measures helps connect stories like the NGO example to broader theme.

For instance, journalists reporting on democracy trends often rely on indexes that summarize many pieces of information into one score (example: US News coverage). These indexes attempt to capture complicated realities—such as the quality of elections, the extent of civil liberties, and the strength of accountability institutions—into numerical scales that can be compared across countries and over time. Some indexes may weigh elections more heavily, while others emphasize freedom of the press or judicial independence. This means that the same country might receive different scores depending on which index you consult, and those differences reflect the choices researchers make about what democracy means and how it should be observed.

Where do these indexes come from? Who collects them? Scholars and reporters often use measures such as:

  • V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy) – global dataset with dozens of democracy indicators.
  • Freedom House – annual Freedom in the World report categorizing countries as Free, Partly Free, or Not Free.
  • Polity IV Project – long-running dataset scoring countries on democratic and autocratic characteristics.

These indexes differ in scope and methodology, so it’s important to pay attention to the sources cited in the news you read, especially when making generalizations or claims.

2.2 Reading a Codebook

Every dataset should come with a codebook: a document that explains what each variable means, how it is measured, and what its values represent. A full dataset will also include a methodology, which describes how the data was collected, coded, and aggregated. Methodology is essential for research, but here we are focusing on the codebook as the starting point for learning how to read and interpret data.

For this module, we merged two datasets (V-Dem and COW IGO data) to create a practice dataset and its codebook. A codebook typically includes:

  • Variable names and labels
  • Definitions of the concepts being measured
  • Coding rules and sources
  • Units of analysis (e.g., country-year)
  • Scale and type of measurement

Example variable: IGO_participation_level describes the extent of a country’s participation in IGOs. It is an ordinal variable, where higher values indicate higher levels of participation. To illustrate, here is a simple bar plot showing the distribution of IGO participation levels across selected countries:

2.2.1 IGO participation level change

Reflection on Understanding Political Data

  • What is the unit of analysis in the provided codebook? Why does this matter?
  • How should we conceptualize and measure gender equality in politics?
  • If we examine Richland County spending data, what would be the most appropriate unit of analysis?
  • Can we directly compare survey waves collected by different organizations? Why or why not?
  • Why is it important to distinguish between different types of data when conducting analysis?

2.3 Made vs. Found Data

Political scientists work with two main types of data:

  • Made (manufactured) Data – collected through surveys or experiments. For example, v2x_gender from V-Dem is based on expert survey. The American National Election Studes a long-running survey program that collects data on voting, public opinion, and political participation in the United States. It provides repeated surveys across different election years, allowing researchers to track change over time while also recognizing that survey design and context can influence responses.

  • Found Data – administrative records or official statistics. For example, Richland County’s public spending records, or official lists of IGO memberships published by ASEAN or the Singapore Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Surveys and experiments generate made (manufactured) data, while governments and organizations generate found data. Both are valuable, but each comes with challenges. Made (manufactured) data may reflect researcher choices in survey design, while found data may reflect bureaucratic or political priorities.

2.3.1 The Richland County’s Zoo budget

One clear example of found data is the Richland County Zoo and Garden budget. This dataset records yearly spending for the zoo as part of the county’s official budget book. The data were not collected for research, but for fiscal accountability and public transparency. When political scientists use such data, they must adapt administrative categories (like departments or fiscal years) into analytical units that make sense for their research questions.

Reflection on Made vs. Found Data

  • How is the Richland County Zoo budget different from survey-based data like v2x_gender?
  • How might coding decisions affect the way data can be analyzed?

2.3.2 Types of Data

In addition to thinking about where data comes from, we also need to classify types of data:

  • Nominal (categories, no order): e_regionpol_6C (region codes).
  • Ordinal (rank order, unequal spacing): IGO_participation_level_ord.
  • Interval (ordered, equal spacing, no true zero): v2x_polyarchy.
  • Ratio (ordered, equal spacing, meaningful zero): e_gdppc (GDP per capita).

Other examples include regime type as nominal, Freedom House categories as ordinal, temperature during protests as interval, and voter turnout percentage as ratio.

Distinguishing between types of data matters because it affects the kinds of analyses we can perform and the conclusions we can draw. We will revisit these in the following unit; for now, you should understand that these are the kinds of details to look for in a codebook.

4 Types of Variables

Below is a picture showing the dataset we talked about earlier (the same one you explored in the codebook). Each row represents one observation (a country in a specific year), and each column is a variable (such as democracy score, IGO membership, or GDP per capita).
- Look carefully at the rows and columns: what information do they contain?
- How could this dataset be presented visually (tables, bar charts, line plots)?
- In what ways might it help us understand politics?

This section will guide you through the basic statistical concepts needed to interpret and use data. First, let’s talk about the types of variables.

4.1 Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio

Understanding data types is the first step in analysis, because it determines which statistical tools are appropriate.

  • Nominal
    • Definition: Categories with no natural order.
    • Example: e_regionpol_6C – each number represents a region (1 = Africa, 2 = Americas, 3 = Asia, etc.).
    • Key point: You can group or count how many countries fall in each region, but it doesn’t make sense to say one region is “greater” or “less” than another.
  • Ordinal
    • Definition: Categories with a meaningful order, but not evenly spaced.
    • Example: IGO_participation_level – coded as Low, Medium, or High depending on how many IGOs a country joins.
    • Key point: You can rank countries from low to high participation, but the jump from “Low” to “Medium” may not represent the same increase as from “Medium” to “High.”
  • Interval
    • Definition: Ordered, evenly spaced numbers, but without a true zero point.
    • Example: year – the calendar year of observation (1990–2015).
    • Key point: The difference between 2000 and 2005 is five years, but “year 0” doesn’t represent the absence of time, so ratios like “twice as many years” don’t make sense.
  • Ratio
    • Definition: Ordered, evenly spaced numbers, with a true zero point. Ratios are meaningful.
    • Example: e_gdppc – GDP per capita (logged).
    • Key point: Because zero represents the absence of GDP, ratios and comparisons make sense—you can say one country’s GDP per capita is twice another’s or calculate meaningful averages.

4.2 Example: University Enrollment Data

When learning statistics, it helps to begin with something concrete. Consider a dataset that records student enrollment by gender, race, residency, and program level. Such information can be broken into categories and numbers that allow us to see patterns and differences.

This example allows us to review how different data types are defined. The table below provides sample variables with their values and a blank column for classifying the data type:

2024 Fall Semester University of South Carolina Political Science Undergraduate Enrollment Demographic

Variable Example Value Data Type
Gender Male: 46.9% / Female: 53.1% Nominal, ratio
Enrollment Status Full-time: 96.9% / Part-Time: 3.1% Nominal, ratio
Class Standing Freshman: 133 / Sophomore: 201 / Junior: 179 / Senior: 211 Ordinal
Enrollment Count 742 Ratio

In this enrollment example, each variable fits a different type. Gender and enrollment status are nominal because they sort students into categories without order. Class standing is ordinal because the categories follow a sequence (freshman → senior), though the “distance” between them isn’t equal. Enrollment count is ratio because it is a true number with a meaningful zero—742 students means twice as many as 371. Notice that percentages like “53.1% female” are also ratio data, since zero percent would mean no students at all.

Recognizing whether a variable is nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio is the first step in choosing the correct statistical tools.

Data Types & Structure — Quick Check

Think about each question and write down your ideas before clicking to see a sample answer.

  1. Why is it important to know whether a variable is nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?
    Variable type determines which summaries and tests make sense. For example, you can take a mean or run a correlation for ratio/interval data, but not for nominal categories. It also guides plot choice (e.g., bar charts for categories, histograms for numeric data).
  2. Why is e_regionpol_6C considered nominal, while IGO_participation_level is ordinal?
    e_regionpol_6C labels regions (Africa, Americas, Asia, etc.) with no natural order—so it’s nominal. IGO_participation_level (Low/Medium/High) has a meaningful order but uneven steps—so it’s ordinal.
  3. What does it mean when a dataset has one row per country-year?
    Each observation combines a specific country and a specific year. This lets us compare countries in the same year and track change over time for each country.
  4. Using a daily-life example, explain how interval differs from ratio.
    Interval scales have equal steps but no true zero (e.g., temperature °C—20°C isn’t “twice as hot” as 10°C). Ratio scales have a true zero (e.g., income $0 means none; $20 is twice $10).

5 Democracy Indexes as Comparative Data

Just as USC publishes enrollment data, political scientists publish measures of democracy. Beyond V-Dem, some well-known indexes include:

  • Polity IV Project (link)
  • Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index (link)

Researchers use these indexes to ask big questions, such as: Are democracies really better governed? which reviews studies comparing how democracies and autocracies perform. The authors explain that democracies often have advantages in accountability and citizen participation, which can lead to better governance—though the outcomes are not always straightforward or guaranteed.

Their article shows that political scientists build on each other’s work over decades to see whether democracy really improves outcomes, and they also point out the limits—such as the fact that many other factors like economic development or institutions can shape governance quality.

5.1 Correlation: Do Democracies Promote Gender Equality?

One of the simplest and most widely used tools in political science is correlation—a way of measuring how closely two variables move together. But just because two factors show a strong relationship does not mean that one causes the other. For example, ice cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in the summer, but eating ice cream does not cause sunburn—the underlying factor is hot weather.

V-Dem researchers examine whether democracies are correlated with higher levels of gender equality (policy brief). They note that many different factors - that democracies often promote gender equality through education, free elections, and stronger representation of women in politics. Tools like gender quotas and female leadership can help, but the impact is greater when institutions are truly democratic. By contrast, some autocracies use quotas mainly for image or legitimacy, without real reforms.

Researchers often build on each other’s work or combine different methods to identify mechanisms—such as whether specific policies, institutional practices, or cultural norms explain why democracies are linked with greater gender equality.

5.1.1 Correlation between Democracy and Gender Equality in 2014

Exploring Relationships Between Variables

This plot shows the relationship between democracy and gender equality using our practice dataset.
- X-axis: Electoral Democracy Index (v2x_polyarchy)
- Y-axis: Gender Equality Index (v2x_gender)
- Each point: One country in the year 2014 (total = 135 countries)

5.1.2 How to Read the Plot

As you look at the line plot, ask yourself:

  • Do countries with higher democracy scores also tend to have higher gender equality?
  • Are the points close together (showing a strong relationship) or scattered (showing a weaker one)?
  • Does the pattern rise upward (positive correlation) or slope downward (negative correlation)?

Tip: A line or scatter plot like this helps visualize whether two variables “move together,” but it does not tell us why.

5.1.3 Think About the Story Behind the Data

Even if we see a strong correlation, that doesn’t mean one variable causes the other.
For example, ice cream sales and sunburns both increase in summer, but ice cream doesn’t cause sunburn—a third factor (temperature) explains both.

Similarly, democracies might have more gender equality, but other factors—like education, wealth, culture, or policy—could also play a role.

Questions to Consider

  • What are the limitations of saying “democracy promotes gender equality”?
  • Could other factors (e.g., economic development, education, or culture) influence the relationship?
  • Are there countries that don’t fit the general trend? What might explain those cases?

6 Moving Toward Descriptive Statistics

To describe patterns more precisely, we use measures of central tendency and spread:

  • Mean: The mean (or average) adds up all the values and divides by how many there are. It gives a sense of the overall level in the dataset—for example, the average democracy score across all countries. However, the mean can be pulled up or down by extreme values. If one country has an unusually high or low score, it can shift the mean even if most countries cluster around the middle.
  • Median: The median is the middle value when all the data points are ordered from lowest to highest. Half of the countries score above it and half below. Unlike the mean, the median isn’t affected by outliers, so it’s often a better way to describe a “typical” case when the data are unevenly distributed.
  • Variance : These tell us how spread out the data are. Variance measures the average squared distance of each value from the mean. In political science, high variance often signals diversity or inequality—for example, large gaps in democracy, gender equality, or income across nations. Low variance means countries are more similar on that measure.

Ask yourself: - Is the average democracy score higher where gender equality is stronger?
- Do outliers make the data more variable or less representative?

6.1 Why Descriptive statistics?

Descriptive statistics help us go beyond simply noticing patterns.
They let us ask whether the relationship is consistent, representative, and meaningful.
Just like in enrollment data or public opinion polls, knowing the average, median, and spread gives us a clearer picture of what’s really happening across countries. In the same way, examining higher education enrollment data helps remind us of important concepts: averages, medians, and variation all provide different but complementary ways of understanding patterns in the data.

6.1.1 Distribution Plot of Gender Equality

Exploring Relationships Between Variables

This plot illustrates the variance in gender equality across states in 2014, based on our practice dataset.

  • X-axis: Gender Equality Index (v2x_gender)

  • Y-axis: Frequency (count) of countries at each level of the Gender Equality Index

  • Each bars: Represents accumulated observations of countries in 2014 (total = 135 countries)

  • Red line: The mean of this observations

After looking at the line plot, we can also explore the distribution of the Gender Equality Index. The plot below shows how often each score appears across countries in a single year (each observation = one country in year 2014). This kind of plot helps us see which levels of gender equality are most common and whether the scores are evenly spread or clustered around certain values.

The red line marks the mean (average) score, and the blue line marks the median (middle) score. Comparing these lines helps us understand whether the data is balanced or skewed.

When reading the distribution plot, focus on:

  • Where most countries fall — the peak of the bar.

  • Whether the data is skewed to the left or right (pulled toward lower or higher values).

  • Whether the mean and median lines overlap (a balanced distribution) or sit apart (a skewed one).

  • If there are outliers — countries with unusually high or low scores.

6.2 Central Tendency - What’s Typical?

When we look at data, the first step is usually to describe it. Descriptive statistics give us a snapshot of what the dataset looks like. Using the example of democracy (EDI) and gender equality, these tools allow us to go beyond the scatterplot and summarize patterns numerically. Below, each concept is explained with a short description.

6.2.1 Summary Statistics table for all countries, 2014

Summary Statistics for EDI and Gender Equality
Variable Mean Median SD Min Max N
EDI (v2x_polyarchy) 0.5553259 0.568 0.2531814 0.043 0.923 135
Gender Equality (v2x_gender) 0.7422836 0.798 0.1819070 0.159 0.958 134

Mean (Average): the sum of all values divided by the total number of observations. In the 2014 table, the mean shows the average democracy (EDI) or gender equality score across all countries—or across regions when grouped by e_regionpol_6C.

Median: the middle value when all countries are ordered from lowest to highest. The median represents the “typical” country, especially when a few countries have very high or low scores that might skew the mean.

Range: the difference between the maximum and minimum values. The range shows how much democracy or gender equality varies among countries—whether most are similar or if there are large gaps between the highest and lowest scores.

6.3 Spread – How Much Do Countries Differ?

Exploring Relationships Between Variables

This plot shows the distribution of democracy of 2014 using our practice dataset.
- X-axis: Electoral Democracy Index (v2x_polyarchy)
- Y-axis: Frequency (count) of countries at each level of the Gender Equality Index - Each bars: Represents accumulated observations of countries in 2014 (total = 135 countries)

Mode: the most frequent value in a dataset. For continuous variables like EDI or gender equality, the mode can be seen by looking at the peak of the distribution plot—the point where most countries cluster. While few countries share the exact same EDI score, the peak of the curve still gives a meaningful sense of where democracy scores are most common. For categorical variables such as e_regionpol_6C, the mode identifies the region with the largest number of countries in the dataset.

6.3.1 GDP per Capita (2014)

GDP per capita?

  • GDP per capita: Measures how much economic output (income or production) each person in a country would receive on average if the total GDP were shared equally. In this dataset, the values are scaled by dividing the actual GDP per capita by 1,000 to make the numbers easier to read and compare.

  • The mean of GDP per capita is 17,588 US dollars. and The United state’s GDP per capita in 2014 is 55,380 US dollors.

Exploring Relationships Between Variables

This histogram displays the distribution of GDP per capita (2014) from our practice dataset, illustrating how income levels vary across countries.

  • X-axis: GDP per capita (in thousands of USD) for each country (e_gdppc). For example, a value of 55 represents approximately $55,000 USD.

  • Y-axis: Percentage of countries within each income range (each bar shows the share of total countries in that range).

  • Red vertical line: Indicates the mean (average) GDP per capita across all countries.

  • Green dashed lines: Show ±1 standard deviation from the mean — roughly the range where about 68% of countries fall.

  • Orange and Purple dotted lines: Represent ±2 and ±3 standard deviations from the mean, showing where approximately 95% and 99.7% of countries lie, respectively.

6.4 Understanding Spread and Variation

Range:The distance between the highest and lowest GDP per capita values. It gives a quick sense of how widely countries differ in income—whether most are close together or far apart. Example: In 2014, the range of EDI was 0.043–0.923, while GDP per capita ranged from $776 to $95,278 USD.

Variance: Measures how far each country’s GDP per capita is from the mean.

  • A small variance means most countries have similar income levels.

  • A large variance means there are big differences between richer and poorer countries.

Standard Deviation (SD): The square root of variance, expressed in the same units (thousands of USD). SD shows how tightly GDP per capita values cluster around the mean:

  • About 68% of countries fall within ±1 SD,

  • About 95% fall within ±2 SDs.

In the GDP plot, if most countries fall within 1 SD of the mean, income levels are fairly similar. A wide spread — where many countries fall beyond 2 SDs — shows that global incomes vary greatly across countries.

6.4.1 Key Concepts and How to Read Them

Concept What It Tells You What to Look At / Plot
Mean (Average) The overall level — add up all values and divide by the number of countries. Shows the “average” democracy or GDP score. Summary statistics or distribution plot with mean line.
Median The middle value when all are ordered from lowest to highest. Helps find the “typical” case, especially when data is skewed. Summary statistics or distribution plot with median line.
Mode The most common or frequent value. For continuous data, look for the peak of the curve. Histogram (the tallest point shows the mode) or summary statistics.
Range How far apart the highest and lowest countries are. Gives a quick sense of spread. Summary statistics table.
Variance Measures how much countries differ from the mean overall. Larger variance = greater differences across countries. Summary statistics.
Standard Deviation (SD) Like variance but easier to read—it’s in the same units as the data. About 68% of countries fall within 1 SD of the mean, and 95% within 2 SDs. Summary statistics, or plot with shaded 1 SD and 2 SD areas around the mean.

6.5 Central Tendency and Spread

Earlier, we examined how democracy (EDI) and gender equality can each be described using basic measures such as mean, median, variance, and standard deviation. These measures fall into two key ideas—central tendency and spread—that help summarize what’s typical in the data and how much countries differ from one another.

  • Central tendency: Mean, median, and mode describe the “typical” value. For example, does the average democracy score align with the median, or do a few extreme countries pull the mean higher or lower than most others?
  • Spread: Range, variance, and standard deviation describe how diverse the data is. A higher variance means greater differences among countries; a smaller one suggests countries are more similar in their levels of democracy or gender equality.
  • Skewness and outliers: Some distributions aren’t perfectly balanced. A few countries with extremely high or low scores can distort the overall picture—for instance, a small number of authoritarian states with high gender equality might make the democracy–equality relationship look stronger than it really is.

6.5.1 Statistical Inference

We’ll cover this in more detail during lecture, but it builds directly on what you’ve learned here. Descriptive statistics—like correlation, mean, and variance—are the first step in analyzing data.

Once you can describe a dataset clearly, you can start asking bigger questions: Do these patterns hold in general? Are these differences likely due to chance? Now that we’ve looked more closely at each index, let’s return to the 2014 correlation plot of EDI and Gender Equality.

Statistical inference is the process of drawing conclusions about a larger population using evidence from a smaller sample.

Exploring Relationships Between Variables

This plot shows the relationship between democracy and gender equality using our practice dataset.

  • X-axis: Electoral Democracy Index (v2x_polyarchy)

  • Y-axis: Gender Equality Index (v2x_gender)

  • Each point: One country in the year 2014 (total = 135 countries)

Even when a correlation looks clear, it doesn’t tell the whole story. To dig deeper, you could consider the following:

  • How consistent is the relationship across different regions or income levels?

  • Are there any outliers—countries that don’t fit the overall trend? Which ones?

  • Does the pattern look strong and stable, or could it be shaped by a few extreme cases?

  • Examine how the relationship changes over time with a line plot or trend chart.

  • Later in the course, you’ll learn how to test whether this relationship is statistically significant, meaning it’s unlikely to appear by chance.

In short, correlation plots are a useful starting point—but political scientists go further by combining visual summaries, descriptive statistics, and inference tests to understand why variables are related and whether that relationship truly holds across cases and time.

  • Why do political scientists use multiple democracy indexes (V-Dem, Polity IV, EIU)?
  • Looking at the democracy–gender equality correlation plot, what patterns and limitations do you see?
  • How would you explain the difference between mean, median, and mode to a classmate?
  • What do you think are the strengths and weaknesses of statistical inference in studying politics?

Discussion — Interpreting EDI & Gender Equality

Reflect first, then click to reveal a concise sample answer.

  1. If you had to extend this analysis beyond 2014, what two plots or tables would you add first (and why) to see whether the EDI–gender relationship is stable over time?
    1) A year-by-year correlation table (and by-region panel) to see whether the EDI–gender correlation rises, falls, or stays steady across years.
    2) A time-series line plot of regional means (EDI and gender on separate panels) to check whether regions move together or diverge.
  2. Looking at the gender-equality distribution (2014) with mean/median lines, what does the spacing between those lines tell you about skewness, and why might that matter for interpreting “typical” countries?
    If the mean > median, the distribution is right-skewed; if the mean < median, it’s left-skewed. Skewness matters because the mean can be pulled by extremes, while the median reflects the “typical” country.
  3. Using the by-region summary table (2014), which region shows the highest consistency in EDI (lowest SD)? What might explain cross-regional differences in average levels and spread?
    Western Europe & North America has the lowest SD in EDI (≈0.032), indicating high consistency. Differences may reflect institutions (electoral rules, rule of law), income, state capacity, and within-region heterogeneity.
  4. Give an example where knowing mean vs. median changes your conclusion about a region’s democracy level. What does that reveal about the distribution?
    In Eastern Europe & Central Asia, the mean EDI (~0.558) is below the median (~0.644). The median suggests a higher typical level of democracy than the mean implies—consistent with left skew.

7 Ethical Use of Data

Think about daily life. You might see a news article about a dictator claiming economic success, with charts and numbers that “prove” everything is improving. But you stop and ask yourself: does this sound right? This is where the ethics of data come in. Data can be powerful, but it can also be misleading when it is selectively presented, manipulated, or taken out of context.

In this section, we look at two perspectives:

  1. When you are presented with data – Always ask: Who collected this data? What are their interests? What biases might be shaping the story?
  2. When you are using data yourself – Think carefully about your own responsibility: How will my choices in collecting, cleaning, and analyzing this data affect the story I tell? Am I being transparent and fair?

7.1 When You Are Presented with Data

When you encounter data—whether in a news article, a government report, or a scholarly paper—it can feel like you are looking at something objective and unquestionable. But data is never neutral. It always reflects the choices of who collected it, how it was gathered, and how it is presented. To interpret data responsibly, you must learn to recognize the stories behind the numbers.

Think about possible biases and interests in the story.
Ask yourself: Who benefits from the data being shown in this way? For example, a government might emphasize declining unemployment rates while ignoring wage stagnation, or an authoritarian leader might highlight “record” agricultural output while concealing food shortages. These selective choices create a narrative that supports particular interests.

Coverage limits matter.
Datasets often exclude important cases. A survey might cover only certain years, omit rural populations, or measure only part of an economy. Each gap shapes the story being told. As the APSA Ethics Principles remind us, researchers must acknowledge the limits of their data and remain transparent about what is included and what is left out.

Privacy and re-identification risks.
Numbers that appear anonymous can still be linked back to individuals if enough detail is present—for example, combining age, gender, and location data. Ethical guidance emphasizes that political scientists should protect confidentiality and anticipate risks of harm to participants, even when formal regulations do not require it.

Regulation gaps.
When rules for data use are weak, powerful actors such as corporations, governments, or platforms may exploit data in ways that threaten fairness, privacy, or even democracy. Predictive policing, voter profiling, or surveillance programs often rely on biased or incomplete datasets. APSA’s ethics statement urges researchers to reflect not only on compliance with laws, but also on their broader responsibility to protect participants and promote integrity in political processes.

The key considerations, always pause and ask:

  • Where does this data come from?
  • What might be missing?
  • Whose voices are excluded?
  • What risks could emerge if this data were misused?

By developing these habits, you can see beyond the surface of a chart or statistic and begin to evaluate the deeper ethical and political questions tied to data.

7.2 When You Are Using Data

As students and researchers, you will not only consume data—you will also produce it, analyze it, and present it to others. This gives you significant responsibility. The stories you tell with data can shape public debates, influence policies, or affect people’s lives. Ethical use of data means recognizing this responsibility and acting with transparency and care.

Respect participants.
When your data involves people, their safety and dignity come first. This means protecting confidentiality, avoiding unnecessary harm, and being mindful of potential re-traumatization when dealing with sensitive topics or vulnerable groups. For example, reporting on survivors of violence requires careful anonymization and sensitivity to context.

Be transparent.
Every dataset is the product of choices: what to collect, how to code, which cases to include, and what methods to apply. Explaining these choices clearly—both in class projects and in published research—allows others to judge the credibility of your work and encourages trust. Transparency also helps others replicate and build on your findings.

Minimize harm.
Consider risks beyond the individual. Publishing data that stigmatizes a community can deepen inequalities or invite discrimination. Ethical practice means actively looking for these risks and making decisions that reduce potential harm wherever possible.

Check fairness.
Be alert to how your methods or interpretations might reinforce bias. Algorithms trained on biased data, selective sampling that overlooks marginalized voices, or framing results in ways that privilege one group all shape unfair outcomes. Strive for fairness by questioning your own assumptions and diversifying the evidence you use.

Accountability.
Your audience, your participants, and the broader public may be influenced by the stories you tell. Accuracy and honesty are non-negotiable. Accountability means owning mistakes, correcting errors, and being clear about the limits of your conclusions.

Long-term impact.
Research findings can echo far beyond the classroom—they can influence policy, shape media coverage, and alter public trust in science. Ethical responsibility requires you to think about how your work might be applied or misused in the future, and to frame your results in ways that balance curiosity with social responsibility.

The key consideration: when you use data, always reflect on your role as a storyteller. The choices you make in collection, analysis, and presentation all shape the narrative. Be transparent about your decisions, protect those represented in the data, and consider the broader impact of your work beyond immediate research goals.

Good practice in political science involves critical reflection, transparency, and accountability, ensuring that data is used to advance knowledge without causing undue harm.

7.2.1 Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and Data

After learning about individual and professional responsibilities in data ethics, it’s important to see how those responsibilities are enforced in practice. Many countries and universities have systems that provide oversight for research involving people. For example, the European Union’s Data Act was created to increase transparency, protect privacy, and ensure that data is used fairly. Policies like this aim to balance innovation with safeguards for individuals and communities.

At U.S. universities, this role belongs to the Institutional Review Board (IRB) — a committee that reviews research projects to make sure they are ethical, voluntary, and low-risk.

IRBs highlight key ethical responsibilities: - Protect participants from unnecessary risks or harm. - Ensure informed consent is obtained whenever possible. - Maintain confidentiality and data security. - Consider long-term consequences of research decisions.

For example, if a student wanted to survey classmates about voting habits, the IRB would check that participation is voluntary, responses are anonymous, and no one feels pressured to take part. At our own university, the University of South Carolina IRB provides guidelines and approvals for any study involving human subjects. This oversight is not meant to stop research, but to make sure that projects are designed responsibly and ethically.

IRBs differ from national laws such as the European Union’s Data Act, which regulates data use for the general public. IRBs focus specifically on research ethics within universities—turning broad principles into clear checks for academic projects.At USC, the IRB is part of the Office of Research Compliance and is responsible for reviewing all human subjects research to ensure it meets federal regulations and ethical standards. This includes evaluating risk levels, requiring informed consent processes, monitoring confidentiality protections, and ensuring that vulnerable populations receive extra safeguards.

Together with your role as a consumer and producer of data, IRBs show the final layer of responsibility: institutions. This completes the circle—ethical data practice involves individual awareness, professional responsibility, and institutional oversight, all working together to protect participants and strengthen public trust in research.

7.3 Key Takeaways

  • Data tells a story—but never the whole story. Always ask what’s behind the numbers.
  • As a consumer of data:stay curious and critical. Question sources, look for bias, and think about what might be missing.
  • As a producer of data: be transparent about your methods, protect participants, and consider how your analysis might affect real people and communities.
  • Ethical responsibility goes beyond personal judgment—it includes systems that promote accountability. Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) provide this oversight by ensuring research is voluntary, safe, and respectful of participants.
  • Together, these layers—individual awareness, professional integrity, and institutional safeguards—build public trust and help ensure that data in political science is used responsibly and for the public good.

Short Answer & Discussion Questions

Think about each question and write down your ideas before clicking to see a sample answer.

  1. If a news article uses a single statistic to make a political point, what questions should you ask?
    Ask about the source, definition, denominator, time frame, measurement, uncertainty, and bias. Also consider alternative indicators or interests of the author.
  2. How can researchers minimize harm when working with vulnerable groups?
    Use informed consent, assess risk, collect minimal data, protect identities, and seek IRB/ethics approval. Engage respectfully with the community and avoid re-traumatization.
  3. How should researchers balance transparency with the need to protect confidentiality?
    Share methods and code but limit sensitive data exposure: use aggregated or de-identified data, add noise or tiered access, and clearly document redactions.
  4. Is it ever acceptable for researchers to use deception in data collection? Why or why not?
    Only when scientifically necessary, no alternatives exist, risks are minimal, and participants are debriefed—subject to IRB/ethics review.
